---
title: "What Changed from the Course Project"
---

This project began as a graduate course group project, submitted in April
2026. The original submission is preserved unchanged in the repository as
the tag
[`v1.0-course-submission`](https://github.com/inukbaik/fomc-policy-modeling/tree/v1.0-course-submission).
This page lists what was changed for the portfolio version, why, and what
each change did to the results.

Numbers below are the results **at the time of each change**, taken from
the commit history. Later changes (and refreshed FRED data) move them, so
the current results are on [The prediction](prediction.qmd).

## Data and reproducibility

- **One data pipeline.** Two hand-run acquisition notebooks were replaced
  by one script, `R/acquire_data.R`, that scrapes the FOMC calendar from
  the Federal Reserve and pulls every series from FRED. It fixed three
  meetings missing from the old calendar (meetings that span two months)
  and a cancelled March 2020 meeting that had been counted. The ICE BofA
  high-yield spread was dropped: FRED now serves only about three years
  of it.
- **Pinned environment.** Package versions are locked with renv.
- **No hardcoded values.** The sample end, structural-break dates and
  gap-filling were hardcoded; they are now computed from the data or set
  in one settings file, so the site survives a data refresh.
- **One site instead of one notebook.** The 2,000-line R Markdown file
  became this Quarto site, with shared code in `R/`. Outputs were checked
  to match before and after.

## The prediction chapter (RQ3)

**Meeting labels.** The original labels came from the change in the
*monthly average* target between meeting months. A move late in one month
raised the next month's average, so later holds were labelled as hikes or
cuts. The labels were wrong for 65 of 323 meetings (84 cuts labelled
against 42 real ones). Labels now come from the daily target around each
scheduled meeting. Much of the original apparent skill disappeared: the
random forest's kappa fell from 0.34 to 0.10, and XGBoost collapsed to
always predicting "hold".

**A fair evaluation.**

- The scoring rule dropped classes a model never predicted, so "always
  hold" was scored on holds alone and ranked first (macro-F1 0.74). Such
  classes now count as F1 = 0, which puts "always hold" last (0.29).
- Models are ranked on the pooled predictions of every expanding-window
  fold, with block-bootstrap intervals, instead of a single 80/20 split.
- Tuning is time-ordered everywhere; elastic net no longer picks its
  penalty with random cross-validation folds.
- Each meeting uses only data published before it (publication delays).
- Class weighting became a tuning choice after fixed weights lowered every
  model's score.
- Two baselines were added. "Same as last meeting" (0.65) beat every model
  at that point.

**Faster runs, identical results.** Running the evaluation folds in
parallel and reusing boosted-tree fits cut a full cold render from 277 s
to 85 s, with every output unchanged.

**Better inputs.** Levels that trend over decades became growth rates,
calendar counts became meeting-based timing, and the models got the
information the strongest baselines rely on: the previous decision, the
direction and age of the last rate change, the target level with a
zero-lower-bound flag, and the 2-year-yield market signal. Pooled
macro-F1 rose from 0.38 to 0.72 for elastic net, 0.43 to 0.67 for the
multinomial logit and 0.55 to 0.66 for XGBoost, putting all three above
"same as last meeting". Momentum features (3-month changes, Sahm rule)
were tried and dropped after they lowered three of four models; the
chapter discloses that this choice used the evaluation results.

**Dynamic models.** An ordered probit with the lagged decision and a
two-step hazard model (a simplified Hamilton–Jordà autoregressive
conditional hazard), both on a small set of inputs fixed in advance. The
hazard model tied the best machine-learning model (0.715).

**Window check.** Refitting every model on only the latest 120 meetings
lowered five of six fitted models clearly: older history helps.

## The rule and the regimes (RQ1, RQ2)

These chapters are the course-project teammates' original analyses. Their
methods were not revised; each now opens with a note on known limitations
(for example, a possibly spurious levels regression in RQ1 and trending
inputs in RQ2). Only shared data fixes and small cleanups touched them.
